Seasonal demand increase coming through 
 The copper price moved sideways in a $9,200-9,900/t range in April, as sentiment 
about demand prospects seesawed between optimism and pessimism.  In early May 
it broke below $9,000/t in a test of downside support. 
 Consumers remain covered with contracted material.  However, prices falling to the 
lower end of the range attracted some spot buying on the dips in April helping push 
up premia slightly in Europe and China. 
 Overall, exchange inventories fell in April. Those in the US accounted for the 
decline, as European and Asian inventories were steady.  However, within Asia LME 
stocks rose while SHFE stocks fell.  Meanwhile, bonded warehouse stocks in 
Shanghai have fallen to leave total estimated and reported stocks down m-o-m.

Demand fears overwhelm 
underlying strength 
April saw the copper price oscillate in a $9,200-9,900/t 
range.  This was due to sentiment about demand 
prospects seesawing between optimism and pessimism.  
The increase in interest rates in Europe by the ECB on 6th 
April was one source of pessimism due to the eventual 
negative impact on final demand for copper.  However, 
the biggest source of concern was the impact of the 
Chinese government’s efforts to tame inflation.  Interest 
rates and reserve ratios were hiked again over the past 
month, and Q1 GDP growth surprised on the high side.  
A series of both lower highs and lows compressed 
copper’s trading range over the past month.  In early May 
this pressure finally led to a decisive break below 
downside support in a broad-based sell off across all 
LME metals, when the official cash price fell to $8,791/t 
on 5th May.  This was despite reports from the physical 
market that underlying demand has been fairly strong. 
Destocking appears to be over 
High copper prices and improved scrap availability prompted significant destocking of cathode in Q1.  This 
happened everywhere, and especially in price conscious China.  We estimate that consumers there reduced 
their cathode inventory by 140,000t in Q1, as the table below indicates.  This was more than offset by the 
estimated build up in bonded warehouse stocks in Shanghai, leaving a net 60,000t increase in off warrant 
stocks in China in Q1.  The bonded warehouse stocks rose because of the increase in collateral stocks as 
outlined in last month’s monitor. 
In April, the drawdown in SHFE stocks continued but bonded warehouse stocks fell by an estimated 
20,000t, driven by a 10,000t decrease in both trader stocks and stocks held by speculators as collateral for 
financing.  We estimate that producer stocks in China remained unchanged while consumer stocks fell 
marginally, as destocking reached its 
lower limit over the past month.  
Therefore, total estimated and reported 
stocks in China fell by 59,000t over the 
past month.  Of course, the collateral 
stocks in China could still be dumped 
onto the market should credit 
conditions tighten enough and make it 
difficult for the holders of this metal to 
roll over their loans.  As reported in 
our last Copper China Fortnightly, a 
tightening of foreign exchange policy 
aimed directly at these deals is unlikely 
to impact these players as most have 
off shore accounts.  However, our

that some of these players sold metal last month, partly as a pre-emptive response to the 
potential of more draconian policy changes that may actually achieve a reduction in the use 
of cathode as a financing tool.  However, we believe that releases of this material back to 
the market will be done gradually, as letters of credit of 3-6 months and other loans come 
due.  In addition, the consumer destocking in China of 140,000t in Q1 leaves a cushion to 
absorb the stock overhang in the country. 
Outside of China, destocking has also run its course, yet consumers still shy away from 
stocking up on expensive copper and are replacing cathode with scrap where they can.  This 
combined with the fact that contracted material was generally sufficient to meet 
requirements has left the spot market quiet.  Premia though ticked higher over the past 
month in Europe, up to $50-90/t from the lows reached in March.  Some buyers came into the market as 
prices fell towards $9,200/t.  In the US, premia have been flat at 5.0-6.5¢/lb, following the freight rate 
induced increases seen last month.  We understand that there was an increase in supply late in the month but 
it has not been enough to undermine the premium. 
Underlying demand for total copper units still strong 
The only modest declines in exchange stocks that we have seen so far in 2011 due to consumer destocking 
are hiding, to an extent, the underlying strength of consumption growth of total copper (that is refined metal 
and copper contained in direct use scrap combined).  At the macroeconomic level, global industrial 
production in Q1 2011 is estimated to have grown by 6.5% y-o-y and is forecast to decelerate only modestly 
to 5.5% in Q2.  Moreover, the anticipated slowdown in the annual growth rate is mainly due to comparisons 
with the peak of the recovery in Q2 2010.  Despite recent increases in interest rates in China and Europe, 
monetary policy remains loose and should support sustained industrial production growth and therefore total 
copper demand. 
Chinese IP growth is forecast to remain strong, as momentum sustains growth despite efforts to cool the 
economy.  The translation of broader economic growth to copper demand is occurring now that consumer 
destocking has run largely its course.  Q2 is the seasonally strong quarter in China (and most other large 
markets in the northern hemisphere).  Wire & cable demand in China is increasing from the seasonally weak 
Q1, with large wirerod producers in China reporting that utilisation rates increased sharply in April.  We 
therefore forecast that Q2 will see an increase in refined consumption in China of over 200,000t, due to a 
broad-based increase in semi fabricated production to meet demand.  This is supported by the draw down in 
SHFE tax-paid stocks to less than 100,000t at the end of April from almost 132,000t at the end of March.  
Our China analyst attributes this decline to increased demand for physical units in China. 
The negative SHFE-LME arbitrage has kept the Chinese spot import premium well below the benchmark 
level of $115/t, having ranged between $40-100/t in April.  The arbitrage is also prompting continued 
exports of cathode from China.  March exports of cathode from China leapt to 36,768t, their highest level 
since December 2005.  We believe that some of this material ended up in LME warehouses in the region.  
For example, Chinese exports to Korea and Singapore increased by almost 23,000t and 10,000t respectively 
in March.  Over the same period, Korean LME warehouse stocks rose by almost 21,000t and those in 
Singapore by over 11,000t.  Korean and Singaporean LME warehouse stocks rose by a further 26,000t in 
April, probably due to continued Chinese exports.  In addition, we understand that some Chinese refined 
exports in April went to Japan to meet requirements there due to the lingering effects of the earthquake and 
tsunami on refined production by the Japanese smelters and refiners. 
Chinese exports are most probably coming from bonded warehouses, as the 17% VAT on tax-paid SHFE 
metal (which is not refundable) makes it uneconomic to use this metal.  The arbitrage remained negative 
throughout April but narrowed significantly to less than $5/t at the end of the month, as LME prices slid and

cathode demand picked up domestically to support SHFE 
prices.  Therefore, we expect to see a slowdown in exports 
in May.  As for imports, they are likely to have risen 
strongly in April, given reports we have received from 
traders of activity over the past month.  Continued growth 
in copper consumption and the narrowing of the negative 
arb is also likely to lead to a further increase in imports in 
May (see chart at right). 
Moves into higher value added sectors 
continue apace 
The semis industry continues to adapt to the high price 
environment.  The proposed purchase by Aurubis of 
Luvata’s flat rolled business is a good example of the 
changes afoot through the copper supply chain.  Aurubis 
moving further downstream to capture more margin fits 
with its integrated copper supplier strategy.  Equally, the 
sale by Luvata of its largely commodity flat rolled business 
also fits with the move by it and many other fabricators to 
become multi-material, higher value added solution 
providers rather than just metal processors.  Of course, the space available for fabricators to move further up 
the chain is limited.  Also, the number of buyers for semi fabricators disposing of non-core commodity 
semis operations is equally limited.  Not many refined producers, particularly miners, are pursuing a strategy 
of moving further downstream. 
Miners continue to suffer from ore grade declines and natural hazards 
Recent Q1 results show that ore grade issues and natural hazards remain the main difficulties facing miners.  
In H1 2011, we anticipate that refined production will grow by only 0.1% y-o-y.  A flattering increase of 
2.3% in Q1, due to comparison with a disrupted Q1 2010, should be offset by an expected decline of 1.9% 
y-o-y in Q2.  In part the decline in refined output in Q2 is based on our historical accuracy and assessment of 
risks, which lead us to consider a mine disruption 
allowance of 7.0% in the quarter.  Also, a year with as few 
disruptions as 2010 does not tend to happen often, and so 
the odds are that 2011 will see a few more problems.  
Support likely to hold and prices rise back 
over $9,000/t 
We expect that the decline in the price to below $9,000/t at 
the time of writing will be followed by a rise back above 
this key level.  In particular, we expect that the underlying 
strength in demand and weak supply growth should lead to 
a large deficit in Q2, which should support prices.  As the 
chart at right indicates, the weakening dollar has provided 
little support to the price so far this year.  Exchange stocks 
are already declining, albeit modestly.  The continued 
translation of the deficit into declines in visible stocks (or 
not) will be the key determinant of the short term price 
direction.

Consumption trends 
Global copper wirerod production 
With most trade and other data for 2010 published we now estimate that global copper wirerod 
production in 2010 grew by 8.1% to 14.0 million tonnes.  This was around 100,000 tonnes above our 
previous estimate due to higher than expected growth in China and other parts of developing Asia and in 
Russia.  Initial data in for the first quarter of 2011 shows that global copper wirerod production grew by 
3.3% to 3.5 million tonnes.  The strongest growth in production was in Europe, where output was up an 
estimated 10.4%.  This was down to a continued recovery in copper wire and cable production but also as 
a result of a rise in net exports, which grew from 84,000 tonnes in Q1 2010 to 132,000 tonnes in Q1 2011.  
In contrast copper wirerod production in China was estimated to have fallen by 0.4% as a result of a 
slowdown in wire and cable production and some destocking in the face of high and volatile copper 
prices.  In North America copper wirerod production continued its slow recovery, but in North East Asia 
output was flat due to falling exports from Taiwan and the problems in Japan.             
Impact of the earthquake and tsunami in Japan 
Whilst the earthquake and subsequent tsunami in Japan caused quite a lot of damage the most important 
issue in terms of long term impact to wire and cable production is related to the ongoing power shortages.  
Efforts are being made to recommission some old idled capacity but currently peak electricity demand is 
still in excess of generation capacity in the North of Japan.  One of the problems is that Japan’s main 
island has two separate electricity grids, one of which operates at 60Hz and the other operating at 50Hz. 
This means that power can only be transferred between the two regions via frequency converters and 
these do not have enough capacity to alleviate the power shortages.  As a result there is a rolling 
programme of power cuts that looks set to last well into this year, with some observes predicting that they 
could last till Q4.  
In terms of wire and cable production around 10% of total capacity was in some way damaged in the 
original disaster, but most of this will be repaired by May at the latest. The main impact was on high 
voltage underground cable and fibre optic cable production (where around 50% of total capacity was 
affected), but since the HV sector uses less than 20,000 tonnes of copper per year and the fibre optic cable 
sector none, these two sectors are not important in terms of overall copper usage. The full impact of the 
power shortages is still unclear but overall we are currently forecasting that wire and cable production in 
Japan will fall by almost 5% this year. 
Unrest in North Africa and the Middle East 
The current unrest in North Africa and the Middle East will have some impact on wire and cable 
production, and hence copper wirerod demand, but unless this spreads to the larger countries of the GCC 
we do not believe this will have a major impact at a global level.  Wire and cable production in Tunisia in 
2010 consumed around 40,000 tonnes of copper with around half of this used in automotive wire, and 
although local consumption of wire and cable has been hit by the political unrest, the automotive sector 
has been relatively unaffected. Libyan wire and cable production is very small with under 6,000 tonnes of 
copper being used in 2010.  Most of the wire and cable used in Libya is imported with net imports in 
2010 representing an estimated 37,000 tonnes of copper content.  Clearly this will be much lower in 2011 
and this will impact on the main exporters to this country.  Egypt is by far the largest wire and cable 
producer in North Africa, with copper cable production of around 117,000 tonnes in 2010.  However, 
much of this is exported to the GCC and increasingly Europe and consumption of copper cable in 2010 in 
Egypt was only around 57,000 tonnes conductor.  Local consumption has been hit by the political unrest,

but the situation does now seem more stable and provided this continues then the market should not be 
too badly affected.  The Syrian market is also quite small and is relatively self contained and the Yemeni 
market is very small, whilst in Bahrain there is no local copper cable production with all the market being 
served by imports.  The Bahrain market in 2010 consumed under 20,000 tonnes of copper conductor 
cable which is under 3% of the total GCC market.  Overall we estimate that the current unrest may cut 
regional copper rod consumption by around 50,000 tonnes in 2011. 
Russian cable industry rebounds in 2010 
After the dramatic slump in 2009 the Russian cable industry staged a recovery in 2010, although output of 
copper wire and cable is still below pre-crisis levels.  Copper cable production grew year-on-year by 
23.5% in H1 2010 and by 19.6% in H2.  The slowdown in H2 was more due to the stronger H2 2009, 
with H2 2010 production 27.2% up on H1 2010.  However, this still left Russian copper cable production 
over 20% down on 2007, and we are forecasting that it will only return to 2007 levels in 2012.  The 
recovery was driven by rising demand for power cables, along with increased consumption of automotive 
wire and winding wire, whilst the building wire sector remained depressed.   
China posts a weak Q1 
It was a slow start to the year in China, although traditionally Q1 is the weakest quarter for the Chinese 
wire and cable sector.  Initial estimates point to a small fall in copper cable production despite an upturn 
in March, with data showing that cable industry capacity utilisation fell significantly in February.  
Government efforts to tighten the availability of credit to help cool inflation, coupled with the high price 
of copper, has resulted in a reduction of working stocks from an average of 11 days in January to 5 in 
March.  The tightening of domestic credit is also causing some concern that it might lead to a rise in bad 
debts.  On top of the destocking, the high price of copper has led to reports of some orders being 
postponed, and all this has contributed to the muted demand in Q1.  Although this slow start to the year 
may lead to overall wire and cable demand growth in 2011 being down on 2010, there is every reason to 
remain optimistic that Q2 will see a return to healthy growth, with more than 60% of wire and cable 
manufacturers holding a positive view on Q2 demand.  The Chinese State Grid is intending to boost 
investment by 10% this year and has ambitious plans to expand the grid between now and 2015.  In some 
parts of the country rising demand for electricity means that current grid infrastructure is struggling to 
meet demand and needs to be upgraded.  Meanwhile there are plans to build 36 million social housing 
units over the next five years, although measures to curb real estate development may start to impact on 
demand for building wire in the second half of this year.  One cloud on the horizon though for copper is 
the news that one utility is now planning to switch much of its cable from copper to aluminium conductor 
to save money. 
Overall cable industry outlook still good 
Despite the negative issues in some parts of the world there is every reason to believe that 2011 will see 
further good growth in the global wire and cable market.  Provided there are no more major shocks the 
developed world is forecast to continue to see a steady recovery in demand, whilst in the developing 
world wire and cable consumption growth also looks positive.  In the two other BRIC’s, Brazil and India, 
wire and cable demand is rising strongly boosted by investment in infrastructure and general economic 
expansion. Looking further ahead the problems with nuclear power in Japan has caused many countries to 
look again at their own nuclear industries and this may well lead to more emphasis being put on other 
forms of low carbon emission generation, most of which use greater volumes of wire and cable than 
nuclear power, both in the actual generation process and in connecting this generation to the grid.

Industry News 
Consumption 
 
It was announced on 29th April that Aurubis AG, the German copper producer and semis fabricator, 
expects to acquire Luvata RPD, the rolled products division of Luvata Group, in August 2011.  An 
acquisition agreement has already been reached.  Aurubis will pay the net working capital of Luvata 
RPD at the time of closing, which is anticipated to be between €200 – 250M. 
 
It was reported that the State Grid Corp. of China is anticipated to invest RMB300B per annum 
from 2011 to 2015 for the construction of power grids.  The project has been approved as part of 
China’s current 5-year plan which dates from 2011 to 2015.  It is anticipated to require between 1.12 
and 1.25Mt of copper. 
 
According to the Japanese Copper and Brass Association, rolled copper product output fell by 
3.7% y-o-y to 68,620t in March.  This was mainly attributed to disruption in automotive supply 
chains following the earthquake on 11th March.  The full impact of the decline of Japanese carmakers 
is expected to hit the copper market in the forthcoming months due to the anticipated two month time 
lag in copper demand.  There is, however, optimism about the medium term demand outlook due to 
growing demand for air conditioners and home appliances in addition to the positive effects of the 
forthcoming reconstruction work.  The impacted operations of automotive component manufacturers 
are expected to recover towards the summer. 
 
Colada Continua Chilena, the Chilean copper wire producer, announced plans to expand the 
capacity of its Continua plant by 40,000t/y to 115,000t/y through the construction of two new 
production lines.  The company anticipates that the first production line will commence operations by 
mid-2012, while the second is likely to follow two or three years later.  Proposals have yet to be 
evaluated from an environmental viewpoint.  It is expected that the cost of the project will amount to 
US$8.0M. 
 
Steel Dynamics and LaFarga Group, the US carbon steel producer and the Spanish copper semis 
fabricator respectively, announced plans for a joint venture that will operate under the name SDI

 
It was reported that Wolverine Tube Inc., the US copper tube producer, signed a memorandum of 
understanding with the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corp. as part of a joint plan of reorganisation to 
emerge from Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection.  The company intends to sell Wolverine Tube 
Europe BV, its Netherlands-based sales and distribution unit in order to fulfil debt obligations 
caused by volatile copper prices and declining sales revenues.  Wolverine Tube Europe BV markets 
copper and copper alloy tube products that are principally used in HVACR applications.   
 
Chinese imports of refined copper and copper products rose to 304,299t in March, up by 29% from 
235,469t in the previous month.  This was mainly attributed to an increase in the production of 
fabricators.  However, the March figure represented a 33% decrease from March 2010. 
 
A joint venture between Statnett and National Grid, the Norwegian and UK grid operators 
respectively, said that it plans to lay 800km of 1,400MW submarine power cable between Norway 
and the UK between 2017 and 2020.  This follows last year’s announcement, outlining Statnett’s 
intention to build four new cable connections to continental Europe with a total capacity of 
4,200MW.  The company expects to invest between US$2.2B and US$2.4B on cable projects until 
2020. 
Mine Production 
 
On 2nd May it was reported that Codelco has allocated US$2.2B until 2019 for expenditure on the 
development of underground deposits at its Chuquicamata open pit copper mine.  Codelco has 
commissioned a feasibility study to transition operations underground by 2018.  2011 production at 
the mine is expected to be 379,000t of copper-in-concentrate and 106,000t of EW cathode. 
 
On 25th April, Canadian mining company Barrick Gold outbid China’s Minmetals Resources’ offer 
for Australian company Equinox Minerals Ltd at a price of US$7.7B.  Equinox Minerals is the 
operator of the Lumwana mine in Zambia and the majority owner of the Jabal Sayid project in 
Saudi Arabia.  Barrick Gold’s offer equates to US$8.57 per share, which is 16% higher than 
Minmetals Resources’ bid and 9% higher than Equinox Minerals’ average share price in the past two 
weeks of trading.  Minmetals subsequently withdrew its offer for Equinox and on 26th April, 
Equinox’s board recommended Barrick’s offer to its shareholders.  Equinox Minerals is expected to 
produce 145,000t of copper-in-concentrate at its Lumwana mine in 2011.  In the same period, 
Barrick Gold is expected to produce 134,000t of EW copper cathode at its Zaldivar mine and 6,000t 
of copper-in-concentrate at its Bulyanhulu operation. 
 
Two workers at the Grasberg copper-gold mine were killed following a flooding incident which 
took place on 18th April in the underground part of the mine.  The incident occurred in the deep ore 
zone (DOZ) of the mine and was caused by sudden and unexpected wet material flows. Operations in 
the DOZ are suspended pending an investigation by the operator, PT Freeport Indonesia, and 
Indonesian authorities.  Operations at the open-pit mine remain unaffected and the mill is running at 
full capacity.  Grasberg is expected to produce around 519,000t of copper-in-concentrate in 2011. 
 
It was announced on 29th April that a deal was nearing completion for higher power prices to be 
imposed on Zambian mining companies, which is set to increase miners’ operating costs. The 
agreement comes in response to Zesco’s appeal for higher prices last year. Zesco, a state-owned 
company, is the main electricity generator to the Copperbelt Energy Corporation, which is in turn 
the leading supplier of power to mines across Southern African nations. The agreement is set for 
completion before the end of the year.

Rio Tinto announced in its Q1 report that copper-in-concentrate output at Escondida was 153,100t 
for the quarter, down 20% y-o-y.  The company stated that the reduction is due to lower than 
expected ore grades.  The average copper ore grade was 1.15%, compared to 1.29% in Q1 2010 and 
1.26% in Q4 2010.  Escondida is expected to produce 723,000t of copper-in-concentrate and 
300,000t of EW copper cathode in 2011. 
 
Adverse mining conditions caused by heavy rains at the Collahuasi copper mine in the Andean 
Highlands, Chile over January and February has resulted in Anglo American announcing that it will 
struggle to meet its 2011 production target.  The company has stated that it has plans to make up for 
the lost output although it has not disclosed a new production target.  Heavy rains and flooding have 
also affected production at Teck Resources' Quebrada Blanca SXEW operation, also in Chile, and 
Xstrata's Tintaya mine in Peru.   
 
Grupo Mexico announced in late April that its Buenavista open pit copper mine, formerly known as 
Cananea, is now operating at full production capacity.  The mine has been increasing its output after 
a long period of worker strike action stretching from July 2007 to June 2010.  Production in 2011 is 
expected to be 75,000t of copper-in-concentrates and 50,000t of EW copper cathode. 
Exploration and Development 
 
Qinghai Weisite Co. Ltd, a subsidiary of the Zijin Mining Group Co. Ltd has announced plans to 
undertake a joint-venture smelting project located in Qinghai province with Western Mining and 
Golmud Shenghua Mining Co. Ltd under the name of Qinghai Copper Co. Ltd. The concentrate 
smelting project aims to reach an annual output capacity of 100,000t/y of copper-in-concentrate and 
the combined investment amounts to RMB800M. A RMB240M cash offer for a 30% stake in the 
project has already been made by Qinghai Copper Co. Ltd. In addition to the aforementioned project, 
Zijin Mining Group Co. Ltd. has already made plans for a 200,000t/y smelting project to be 
completed this year in the Fujian province of China.  Zijin Mining Group produced around 80,000t of 
copper-in-concentrate and around 8,000t of EW copper cathode at its Chinese mining operations in 
2010. 
 
On 19th April, Southern Copper Corporation announced that it would seek talks with the new 
Peruvian government after the final presidential run-off in early June regarding the cancellation of its 
Tia Maria project in Peru.  This came after the current government announced the cancellation of 
the project on 9th April after ruling that the environmental impact assessment filed by SCC was 
“inadmissible”.  In the days before the announcement, three people had been killed in violent protests 
against the project. Tia Maria was expected to produce 120,000t/y of EW cathode at full capacity and 
was due to start-up in 2012, with an investment of US$1B.  
 
On 21st April, Sandfire Resources commenced construction of its Degrussa underground copper-gold 
project in Western Australia. The blasting is hoped to identify the decline necessary for access to the 
underground ore body.  This follows board approval for the project’s development at the end of 
March after the completion of a positive pre-feasibility study which indicated a potential production 
capacity of 68,000t/y of copper ore.  Sources of project finance are yet to be announced and a full 
feasibility study has not yet been undertaken, however the company expects first ore production to 
take place on Q1 2012 and the project to have ramped up to full production by April 2013.  Current 
proven and probable reserves are sufficient for a 7-year mine life.

Smelting and Refining 
 
Mitsubishi Materials Corp, Japan’s third-largest copper producer, announced on 7th April that it 
plans to resume partial operations of its Onahama smelter in mid-July.  The facility has been closed 
since sustaining damage during the disaster and the company declared force majeure on copper-in-
concentrates supply contracts on 14th March.  We expect annual copper cathode production for 2011 
to be at 109,000t (down 53% y-o-y). 
 
Japan’s largest smelter and refiner, Pan Pacific Copper Co. (PPC), said on 6th April that it plans to 
reduce refined copper output in April to September this year by 12% y-o-y to 257,494t.  This is 
mainly attributed to a decrease in production at the Hitachi refinery in the Ibaraki prefecture of 40% 
y-o-y to 53,430t due to the earthquake and tsunami in March.  The company expects to resume 
operations at the Hitachi plant in late April while its Saganoseki and Tamano refineries are now 
operating at full capacity. This follows PPC’s announcement which was reported in last month’s 
Monitor that it would be extending the production cut at its smelting and refining operations into the 
2011/2012 financial year, with a likely increase to raise the cut to 15% of total refined capacity.  This 
reduction thus represents only a small cutback from its previous plan due to some reallocation of 
refined production from Hitachi to Saganoseki and Tamano.  PPC operates the Tamano smelter and 
refinery, the Saganoseki smelter and refinery and the Hitachi refinery, with a total capacity of 
620,000t/y refined copper. 
 
It was announced on 14th April that the Supreme Court of Chile rejected requests to close Codelco’s 
Ventanas plant.  The plant had allegedly released abnormal emissions of SO2 on 23rd March leading 
to the intoxication of 46 people.  The incident occurred while facilities were re-starting operations 
following a maintenance closure. A previous court order to temporarily close Codelco’s Ventanas 
smelter and refinery was suspended on 31st March, a day after it was served.  The company was 
reported on 13th April to be considering closing down the smelter at the site due to its operating at a 
loss and the controversy over its use.  The plans would maintain operation of Ventanas refinery 
which produces 365,000t/y of refined copper.
